afar.e: From Middle English afer, equivalent to a- (“for, on, or of”) + far.
afar.g: At, to, or from a great distance; far away; distantly.

affair.e: From Middle English afere, affere, from Old French afaire, from a- + faire (“to do”), from Latin ad- + facere (“to do”).
affair.g: Something which is done or is to be done; business of any kind, commercial, professional, or public.

affect.e: From Middle English affecten, from Latin affectāre, from Latin affectus, the participle stem of Latin afficere (“to act upon, influence, affect, attack with disease”), from ad- + facere (“to make, do”). By surface analysis, af- + Latin -fect.

From Middle English affecten, from Anglo-Norman affecter (“strive after”), Middle French affecter (“feign”), and their source, Latin affectāre (“to strive after, aim to do, pursue, imitate with dissimulation, feign”), frequentative of afficere (“to act upon, influence”) (see Etymology 1, above).
affect.g: To make a show of; to put on a pretense of; to feign; to assume. To make a false display of.

affection.e: From Middle English affection, affeccion, affeccioun, from Old French affection, from Latin affectiōnem, from affectiō; equivalent to affect + -ion.
affection.g: The act of affecting or acting upon.

affinity.e: From Middle English affinite, from Old French affinité. Ostensibly equivalent to affine + -ity.
affinity.g: A natural attraction or feeling of kinship to a person or thing.

affirm.e: From Middle English affermen, from Old French afermer, affermer, from Latin affirmare, adfirmare (“to present as fixed, aver, affirm”), from ad (“to”) + firmare (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”). By surface analysis, af- + firm.
affirm.g: To agree, verify or concur; to answer positively.

affix.e: Borrowed from Latin affixus, perfect passive participle of affigere (from ad- + figere). By surface analysis, af- + fix.
affix.g: A bound morpheme added to a word’s stem, such as a prefix or suffix.

afflict.e: From Middle English afflicten (attested in past participle afflicte), from Latin afflīctō (“to damage, harass, torment”), from ad- + flīctus, past participle of afflīgō (“strike, beat”), from ad- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence af-).
afflict.g: To cause (someone) pain, suffering or distress.

affliction.e: From Middle English affliction, affliccioun, from Old French afliction, borrowed from Latin afflīctiōnem (“pain, suffering, torment”), from Latin afflīctō (“to damage, harass, torment”), from ad- + flīctus, past participle of afflīgō (“strike, beat”), from ad- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence af-). By surface analysis, afflict + -ion.
affliction.g: A state of pain, suffering, distress or agony.

afford.e: From Middle English afforthen, aforthen, avorthien, from earlier iforthen, iforthien, ȝeforthien, from Old English forþian, ġeforþian (“to further, accomplish, afford”), from Proto-Germanic *furþōną, from Proto-Germanic *furþą (“forth, forward”), equivalent to a- + forth.
afford.g: To incur, stand, or bear without serious detriment, as an act which might under other circumstances be injurious; (usually after an expressi

affright.e: From Middle English afrighten, from Old English āfyrhtan, equivalent to a- + fright.
From Middle English afright, from Old English āfyrht (“terrified; afraid”), past participle of āfyrhtan (“to terrify; make afraid”).

afore.e: From Middle English afore, aforn, from Old English onforan or ætforan; equivalent to a- + fore.

aforehand.e: From Middle English aforehande, equivalent to afore- + hand.

aforetime.e: From Middle English a fore tyme, afore tyme, aforetyme, afortym, a-for-tyme, afortymez; equivalent to afore- + time.
aforetime.g: In time past; in a former time; formerly.

afraid.e: From Middle English affrayed, affraied, past participle of afraien (“to affray”), from Anglo-Norman afrayer (“to terrify, disquiet, disturb”), from Old French effreer, esfreer (“to disturb, remove the peace from”), from es- (“out”) + freer (“to secure, secure the peace”), from Frankish *friþu (“security, peace”), from Proto-Germanic *friþuz (“peace”).
afraid.g: Impressed with fear or apprehension; in fear.

afresh.e: From Middle English a-fresche, equivalent to a- + fresh.

after.e: From Middle English after, from Old English æfter, from Proto-West Germanic *aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after, *aftiri, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epoteros (“further behind, further away”), from *h₂epo (“off, away”). The Irish usage to indicate recent completion of an activity is a calque of the Irish collocation Táim tar éis...

afterbirth.e: From after- + birth (in the sense of delivery).
afterbirth.g: The placenta and other material expelled via the birth canal following childbirth or parturition in mammals.

afternoon.e: From Middle English afternone, after-non, equivalent to after- + noon.
afternoon.g: The part of the day from noon or lunchtime until sunset, evening, or suppertime or 6pm.

afterward.e: From Middle English afterward, from Old English æfterweard; equivalent to after + -ward.

afterwards.e: From Middle English afterwardes, from Old English æfteweard (“behind”) + -s (“(adverbial genitive)”). By surface analysis, after + -wards.
afterwards.g: At a later or succeeding time; after that;
